In brief

The spectacle of the condemned man tenderly embracing his fiancée on the scaffold gives way to a no less moving development: "A most romantic incident occurred when a handsome young Oxford graduate, noted for his chivalry towards the fair sex, stepped forward and, presenting his visiting card, bankbook and genealogical tree, solicited the hand of the hapless young lady, requesting her to name the day, and was accepted on the spot." Joyce here paints with a broad satirical brush, but he found the essential facts in the biography of Sarah Curran. Two years after Robert Emmet's execution she married an Englishman descended from a noble family.

At more length

Sarah Curran (1782-1808) was the daughter of an Anglo-Irish barrister who became famous for defending the United Irishmen in court. After he forbade her to marry Robert Emmet the couple became secretly engaged in 1803. Living in Cork after Emmet's death later that year, Sarah met a British army captain named Henry Sturgeon, and the couple married in November 1805. Living with her husband at his posting in Sicily, Sarah gave birth to a son after a difficult labor. The boy died only a month after his birth and she died of tuberculosis in May 1808. These facts paint the portrait of a strong-minded but most unfortunate young woman.

Joyce invented the detail of an Oxford education: Captain Sturgeon graduated from the Royal Military Academy before serving with distinction in the Napoleonic wars. The mention of a "genealogical tree," however, and the explanation in the next sentence that the young man is "the bearer, by the way, of one of the most timehonoured names in Albion's history," are rooted in fact. Henry was the nephew of Charles Watson-Wentworth (1730-82), the 2nd Marquess of Rockingham. Lord Rockingham was a Whig statesman who led the House of Lords and served two terms as the Prime Minister of Great Britain. As a Whig leader he was pro-American and pro-Irish, but Sarah's decision to ally herself to English military and political power after being engaged to one of Ireland's most famous revolutionaries caused consternation among Irish nationalists.

She was of course free to marry someone else after Emmet's death, and her choice of an Englishman was not remarkable (both she and Emmet were born into Anglo-Irish families), but nationalists found the fact hard to reconcile with the romantic image created by Emmet's friend Thomas Moore in "She is far from the land." That lyric, touted by the Citizen in the sentence that the parody mocks, makes Sarah an icon of eternal constancy: "She is far from the land where her young hero sleeps, / And lovers are round her, sighing; / But coldly she turns from their gaze, and weeps, / For her heart in his grave is lying." The song promises that not for "long will his Love stay behind him." In fact it took only five years, but a marriage inconveniently filled the interim.

In "The Broken Heart," one of the sketches in The Sketch Book (1864), Washington Irving perpetuates Moore's portrait of a woman "dying of disappointed love," describing her inconsolable suffering at some length, but he allows for the fact of her marriage: "The story of one so true and tender could not but excite great interest in a country remarkable for enthusiasm. It completely won the heart of a brave officer, who paid his addresses to her, and thought that one so true to the dead, could not but prove affectionate to the living. She declined his attentions, for her thoughts were irrevocably engrossed by the memory of her former lover. He, however, persisted in his suit. He solicited not her tenderness, but her esteem. He was assisted by her conviction of his worth, and her sense of her own destitute and dependent situation, for she was existing on the kindness of friends. In a word, he at length succeeded in gaining her hand, though with the solemn assurance, that her heart was unalterably another’s." Sarah proves "an amiable and exemplary wife," but she cannot overcome the grief gnawing her from within and dies "the victim of a broken heart."

Others in the 19th century, however, found it impossible to reconcile Sarah's love with her marriage. Gifford, drawing on a 1976 JJQ article by Fritz Senn, quotes from Irish novelist and politician Justin Huntly McCarthy's Ireland Since the Union (1877): "It is curious to reflect that the three women whose names are associated with the three greatest figures of that revolutionary movement—the wife of Lord Edward Fitzgerald, the wife of Wolfe Tone, and the affianced bride of Robert Emmet—should each have injured the memory of the great men with whose lives they were associated by consenting to accept the love and names of others." Slote, Mamigonian, and Turner quote further from McCarthy: "It is melancholy to have to record the fact that the betrothed wife of Robert Emmet was not entirely faithful to his memory. She married, at the instance, it is said, of her friends, and did not long survive her marriage." The writer manages to suggest that Sarah's early death was a punishment for her infidelity.

Joyce does not bother to give Sarah either a good death or a bad death. He simply pushes the seeming contradiction in her two engagements to ludicrous extremes. The "romantic incident" of a beautiful young woman accepting a second proposal of marriage while her first fiancé awaits torture and decapitatation sends the assembled crowd into transports of sympathetic joy. Perhaps some of the savage mockery is directed at the historical Sarah Curran: the presiding army officer refers to her (affectionately) as "that there bleeding tart." But the main object of Joyce's scorn, here as in all the other Cyclops parodies, is surely the nationalistic chauvinism embodied in the Citizen. Half a million people turn out to see a native son brutally slaughtered by the English occupiers, and in an instant the same patriots cheer no less enthusiastically as his fiancé abandons him for an Englishman.

Speaking of people's sympathetic response to Sarah's suffering, Washinton Irving calls Ireland "a country remarkable for enthusiasm." Joyce may taken a cue from Irving in describing a crowd "rocked with delight" and then "overcome with grief," "touched to the inmost core," convulsed by "heartrending sobs." But he had his own axe to grind. Stephen Dedalus says in part 5 of A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man that Ireland is "the old sow that eats her farrow": "No honourable and sincere man...has given up to you his life and his youth and his affections from the days of Tone to those of Parnell but you sold him to the enemy or failed him in need or reviled him and left him for another." Sarah Curran is not someone to celebrate for patriotic idealism. Nor is she a faithless female. She is, as "Sheila," a symbol of Ireland itself: idealistic, courageous, calculating, and mercenary.

John Hunt 2026
